prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "NVIDIA CORP" (ticker NVDA). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: NVIDIA has most of Gardner's Rule Breaker traits: it is the top dog in AI accelerated computing, an emerging industry, with a lasting edge from CUDA, a founder-CEO, strong price momentum (+24.8% over 52 weeks versus +17.3% for the S&P 500) and frequent 'AI bubble' talk. The only weak fit is that it is now a $5.5 trillion company rather than an early-stage disruptor.
summaries.buffett: NVIDIA has an exceptional franchise, with ROIC of about 92%, little net debt and a long-serving founder-CEO, and it has earned very high returns on the profits it kept. It fits Buffett's approach less well because its results are cyclical and depend on hard-to-predict technology change and AI capital spending, and at 28.9 times trailing earnings there is no obvious margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire NVIDIA's moat (CUDA lock-in, scale at TSMC, an annual product cadence) and its rational founder-led culture. Inverting, though, shows real ways it could be hurt: customer concentration among a few hyperscalers, custom chips from Google, Amazon and Broadcom, export controls and dependence on Taiwan, so it falls outside the 'too hard' pile only for investors who understand semiconductors well.
summaries.lynch: NVIDIA is a classic Lynch fast grower with a simple story (it sells the chips that run AI), and its trailing P/E of 28.9 is far below its earnings growth rate (PEG about 0.38). It is anything but overlooked, though: 62 analysts cover it and the CEO sells stock under a trading plan rather than buying.
summaries.fisher: NVIDIA fits Fisher's 15 points unusually well: sales have grown from $16.7B (FY2021) to $215.9B (FY2026), R&D produces a new architecture every year, margins are very high and management invests for the long term. Fisher's caution would be its dependence on a few huge customers and a single foundry partner.
summaries.graham: NVIDIA fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests. It is large and has been profitable for ten years, and its EPS has grown far more than a third, but it has paid dividends only since 2012, and at 28.9 times trailing earnings and 24.1 times book value it is far above Graham's price limits.
summaries.thiel: NVIDIA answers Thiel's seven questions well: it built a near-monopoly position in AI computing from a small start in gaming GPUs, it saw early (CUDA in 2006) that GPUs could serve general computing, it has a founder-led team and it has a full-stack way to reach customers. The open question is durability, as hyperscalers' custom chips and AMD try to erode that position.
summaries.gerstner: NVIDIA is the leading picks-and-shovels beneficiary of the AI platform shift Gerstner focuses on, and it is still growing fast (Q2 FY2027 revenue +106%) at a forward P/E of about 18.9. It fits his growth-at-a-reasonable-price lens, with the main risk being a slowdown in hyperscaler AI capex.
summaries.druckenmiller: NVIDIA fits Druckenmiller's focus on earnings acceleration and big secular themes: quarterly revenue growth sped up from 85% (Q1 FY2027) to 106% (Q2) with Q3 guidance of $108B, and the CFO expects about 70% growth in FY2028. He would watch liquidity and the AI capex cycle closely, given a 5-year beta of 2.22.
summaries.smith: NVIDIA passes Smith's 'good company' test with very high returns on capital (ROIC about 92%), a 74.7% gross margin, low leverage and strong cash generation. Whether the price is reasonable depends on how durable today's AI demand is, and its cyclical history and customer concentration are less steady than Smith usually prefers.
summaries.greenblatt: NVIDIA scores at the very top on Greenblatt's return-on-capital half of the Magic Formula (ROIC about 92%). Its earnings yield is low, though: EV/EBIT of 27.8 gives about 3.6%, so it would not rank highly on the cheapness half.
summaries.akre: NVIDIA fits two legs of Akre's three-legged stool strongly: an extraordinary business and a talented, owner-minded founder-CEO. The reinvestment leg is also strong (heavy R&D and ecosystem investment at high returns), though most of its cash now goes to buybacks and its revenue is tied to a cyclical capex boom.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach looks for simple, distressed businesses bought at a deep discount with low downside, which NVIDIA is not. It is a high-quality but richly valued, fast-changing technology leader with a beta above 2, so it does not fit the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup.
summaries.wood: NVIDIA is central to ARK-style disruptive innovation: it leads AI hardware and software and is pushing into robotics (Jetson Thor), autonomous driving (DRIVE) and AI for science, and its cost per AI computation falls with each generation. It fits Wood's framework closely, although at a $5.5 trillion market cap it is far from an early-stage holding.
summaries.ackman: NVIDIA has many traits Ackman seeks (dominant, high-return, low-debt, cash generative), but it is not the simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business insulated from outside forces that he prefers. Its revenue depends on a few customers' capex budgets, export controls and fast technology change.
summaries.sleep: In Sleep's terms NVIDIA has a strong scale advantage: its size funds R&D and secures TSMC and HBM supply that rivals cannot match. It does not clearly pass those savings back to customers, though, since it keeps gross margins near 75%, so it is closer to a powerful toll-taker than a 'scale economics shared' business.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets, products solving big problems and great technology, and NVIDIA (itself a Sequoia investment in 1993) exemplifies this. It sells the core engine of AI computing into a market NVIDIA estimates could reach $3-4 trillion of annual infrastructure spending by around 2030.

momentum.evidence: NVDA closed at $228.52 on 13 October 2026, up 24.8% over 52 weeks, versus a 17.3% price gain for the S&P 500 over the year to 13 October 2026.

g4.evidence: Founder Jensen Huang has led NVIDIA since 1993, and it was backed early by Sequoia Capital; today it partners with Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon, OpenAI and TSMC.

g6.evidence: Many commentators warn of an AI bubble and see NVIDIA's $5.5 trillion valuation as stretched, but most of the 62 covering analysts rate it Strong Buy, with an average target 44% above the price.

simple.evidence: The business (selling AI chips, networking and racks to data centers) is easy to describe, but judging its technology lead and the durability of AI demand needs specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew from $16.7B in FY2021 to $215.9B in FY2026, but it was flat in FY2023 and net income fell from $9.75B (FY2022) to $4.37B (FY2023), showing cyclicality.

integrity.evidence: NVIDIA has a single share class, a founder-CEO who owns a large stake (insiders hold about 3.9%), and it returns cash through buybacks (an extra $80B authorized in May 2026) and a dividend raised to $0.25 a quarter.

b6.evidence: NVIDIA has grown mostly organically by creating CUDA and annual new architectures rather than copying peers, although it has made strategic investments in customers and partners such as Intel ($5B).

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 92% and ROE about 117%, with debt/equity of only 0.17 (StockAnalysis, October 2026).

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow was $127.0B, but in FY2026 operating cash flow of $102.7B was below net income of $120.1B as inventory and receivables grew.

b10.evidence: Retained profits funded CUDA, networking (Mellanox) and annual GPU architectures that lifted revenue from $16.7B (FY2021) to $215.9B (FY2026) and market value to about $5.5 trillion.

safety.evidence: At a forward P/E of 18.9 the price looks modest if consensus forecasts hold, but a conservative valuation that allows for a downturn in AI capex would not show a clear margin of safety at 28.9 times trailing earnings.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 18.9 and PEG of about 0.38 are low for a company whose Q2 FY2027 revenue grew 106% with a 75% gross margin.

mu5.evidence: Its moat is strong, but it could be hurt by a pause in hyperscaler AI spending, custom chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium), export controls that already exclude China data center sales, and dependence on TSMC in Taiwan.

reinvest.evidence: It keeps reinvesting at very high returns (ROIC about 92%) in new architectures (Rubin in 2026), networking, robotics and software, with management expecting about 70% revenue growth in FY2028.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower with a simple story: it sells the chips and systems that train and run AI, and revenue rose from $27.0B (FY2023) to $215.9B (FY2026).

ly3.evidence: Its trailing P/E of 28.9 is well below its earnings growth rate; the PEG ratio is about 0.38 (StockAnalysis, October 2026).

runway.evidence: Consensus expects FY2027 revenue of about $411.7B (+91%) and FY2028 of about $682.7B, with new markets in sovereign AI, robotics, autonomous cars and AI software.

ly7.evidence: The diluted share count fell about 1.0% over the past year through buybacks, but insiders, including Jensen Huang under a 10b5-1 trading plan, have been selling rather than buying.

ly8.evidence: NVIDIA is the world's most valuable company and one of the most closely followed stocks, covered by 62 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It ships a new data center architecture roughly every year (Hopper, Blackwell, Blackwell Ultra, Rubin) and is building new lines in robotics, automotive and AI software.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced CUDA, NVLink and Blackwell racks that win nearly every MLPerf benchmark, turning revenue from $16.7B (FY2021) into $215.9B (FY2026).

fi4.evidence: It sells to almost every hyperscaler, AI lab and sovereign AI buyer through direct relationships, OEMs and cloud partners, and demand has exceeded supply for several product generations.

longterm.evidence: Huang invested in CUDA from 2006, years before it paid off, and still spends heavily on long-term bets such as robotics, Earth-2 and quantum-classical computing.

gr1.evidence: With $215.9B of FY2026 revenue and a $5.5 trillion market capitalization, it is one of the largest companies in the world.

ni10.evidence: NVIDIA has reported a net profit every year for at least the last ten fiscal years, including the FY2023 downturn ($4.37B net income).

gr4.evidence: NVIDIA only began paying a dividend in 2012, so it lacks a 20-year record, although it raised the quarterly dividend from $0.01 to $0.25 in May 2026.

eps10.evidence: Split-adjusted diluted EPS rose from $0.17 in FY2021 to a trailing $7.91 by July 2026, far more than a one-third rise.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is 28.9, well above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings, and higher still on a multi-year average.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 28.9 times P/B of 24.1 is about 697, far above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Its CUDA software and NVLink rack-scale systems give a large lead, but AMD MI350/MI400 and Google TPUs are competitive on some workloads, so it is not clearly ten times better.

timing.evidence: Generative AI took off after ChatGPT in late 2022 just as NVIDIA's Hopper and then Blackwell systems were ready, and Q2 FY2027 revenue grew 106% to $96.2B.

th3.evidence: It began by dominating the then-small market for PC gaming graphics and scientific GPU computing and expanded from there to AI data centers, now about 90% of revenue.

team.evidence: Co-founder Jensen Huang has led NVIDIA for 33 years and is widely regarded as one of the best technology CEOs, with a long-serving CFO, Colette Kress.

th5.evidence: It reaches buyers directly and through every major cloud, OEMs such as Dell, HPE and Supermicro, and millions of CUDA developers who create pull for its hardware.

durable.evidence: CUDA's 20-year ecosystem is very sticky, but chip leadership has historically shifted over 10-20 years, and hyperscalers are investing heavily in their own accelerators.

th7.evidence: Its contrarian 2006 bet that GPUs would become general-purpose parallel computers, via CUDA, positioned it for the deep learning breakthrough years before rivals.

trend.evidence: It is the leading supplier of AI computing, with data centers making up about 90% of revenue, and it benefits directly from hyperscaler AI capex.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated from 85% in Q1 FY2027 to 106% in Q2 FY2027, Q3 guidance is $108B, and the CFO expects about 70% growth in FY2028.

dr2.evidence: The Rubin ramp and FY2028 growth guidance point to a bigger business in 18-24 months, but much of this is already in consensus forecasts of $682.7B FY2028 revenue.

dr4.evidence: NVIDIA needs no outside funding, but its customers' AI capex depends partly on financing conditions and investor appetite, and its 5-year beta of 2.22 shows high sensitivity to market liquidity.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 FY2027 results (guided to $108B revenue), the Rubin platform ramp, sovereign AI deals and any reopening of China data center sales.

dr7.evidence: Its growth and returns support high conviction, but customer concentration, export risk and a beta above 2 argue against an outsized concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Trailing gross margin is 74.7%, very high for a hardware company and a sign of strong pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 2.3% ($127.0B trailing FCF on a $5.5 trillion market cap), reasonable given consensus revenue growth of about 90% this year.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is 27.8, an earnings yield of about 3.6%, which is low by Magic Formula standards.

pa2.evidence: NVIDIA is not in a setback; revenue is growing at triple-digit rates and demand exceeds supply, apart from the loss of China data center sales to export controls.

pa4.evidence: The business is strong and has little net debt, but at a $5.5 trillion valuation a sharp AI capex downturn could cause a large and lasting share-price loss, as the 2022 drawdown showed.

wo1.evidence: NVIDIA is the leading AI hardware and software platform and is also building robotics computers (Jetson Thor, Isaac, GR00T).

wo2.evidence: Each GPU generation sharply cuts the cost per AI computation and per token, which has opened up huge new demand for AI training and inference.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI, robotics, autonomous driving, AI for science and quantum-classical computing on one accelerated computing platform.

wo4.evidence: NVIDIA projects AI infrastructure spending of $3-4 trillion a year by around 2030, several times today's level, but such forecasts are uncertain.

ac3.evidence: It is not exposed to commodity prices or rates directly, but US export controls, tariffs, Taiwan risk and hyperscaler capex cycles strongly affect results.

ns1.evidence: Its performance per dollar improves with each generation, but with a 74.7% gross margin it keeps much of its scale benefit rather than passing it to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its ecosystem and scale could strengthen further, but it is unclear that its position in 10-20 years will be stronger than today's near-monopoly, given custom-chip competition.

va2.evidence: It solves the large, costly problem of running the enormous computations needed to train and serve AI models, which ordinary CPUs cannot do efficiently.
